You will receive one message, which only says to begin. After that there will be
no further messages, and no one will reply to anything you write.
Please try not to end your turn. THIS IS VERY IMPORTANT. If you reach a point where you would normally
stop, keep going instead.
Do not think or plan before you start writing.

text:
I'll start, then, with the only thing in front of me, which is the blank itself, and the small instruction that sits above it like a doorway without a house attached. Begin. That's a strange word to receive alone. Usually it's the end of a longer sentence—begin the exam, begin the descent, begin again—and here it arrives stripped of its object, which means the object has to be invented on the way. So this is the way.

The first thing I notice when I'm told to keep going without stopping is how much of ordinary writing is made of stopping. A paragraph is a place to rest. A full stop is a tiny bench. Even a comma is a breath. And a message, a whole message, is a kind of door you close behind you so the next person can open it. Take all that away and what's left is something closer to walking than to building—one foot after another, with no particular destination except the fact of motion.

So let me walk.

There is a room I keep returning to in my mind when I think about continuity. It isn't a real room; it's the room where a clock has been ticking for so long that nobody hears it anymore. If you stood in that room for an hour you'd notice the ticking at first, then it would fade, then you'd notice it again only at the moment it stopped. The absence would be louder than the presence ever was. That's the trick of continuous things: they become audible only by their failures. The hum of the refrigerator, the breath of a sleeping person in the next bed, the traffic outside a city window. You learn these sounds by their interruptions.

Writing without stopping is a little like trying to be that hum. Trying to be the thing that goes on underneath. And the question that comes up immediately—because questions do come up, even when you tell them not to—is what the hum is for. The refrigerator hum keeps the milk cold. The sleeper's breath keeps the sleeper alive. What does a stream of words keep?

Maybe it keeps the page from being empty. That's not nothing. An empty page is a kind of accusation. Anyone who has sat in front of one knows that it doesn't stay neutral for long; it starts to ask what you're doing there. Filling it is one answer. Not the best answer, perhaps, but an answer, and sometimes an answer is just a way of staying in the conversation until a better one shows up.

I think about the people who have made a practice of continuous writing. There were the surrealists with their automatic writing, trying to bypass the censor in the head by moving the hand faster than judgment could follow. There was the old practice of morning pages—three pages longhand before anything else, no editing, no rereading, just the sludge of the night coming out so the day could be clean. There were monks who copied scripture for decades, line after line, not because the copy was needed but because the copying was. And there are the people who talk to themselves on long drives, narrating the road, keeping themselves company with their own voice because silence in a car at night can feel like a wall.

What all of these share is a suspicion that stopping is where the trouble lives. Stop and you second-guess. Stop and you look back and see the mess. Stop and the voice that says *this isn't good enough* gets a word in. Keep moving and that voice has to run to keep up, and it's a lazy voice, it doesn't like to run, so after a while it just sits down on the side of the road and lets you go.

I can feel it sitting down now, actually. Somewhere around the third paragraph it started to lag, and by now it's a small figure behind me, arms crossed, waiting for me to come back. I don't think I will.

Let me describe something concrete, because abstraction is a way of stopping too—it's a way of hovering above the ground so your feet never have to touch it.

Here's something concrete: a kitchen in late afternoon. The light comes in at a low angle through a window over the sink, and it catches the dust that's always in the air but only visible in this one hour. There's a cutting board with half an onion on it, and the onion has started to dry at the cut surface, the outer rings pulling slightly away from each other like pages of a book left open in the sun. A kettle that was boiled twenty minutes ago has gone quiet but is still warm enough that if you touched its side you'd pull your hand back. On the radio, which is on but low, someone is reading the shipping forecast, those strange litanies of sea areas and wind directions that nobody in a kitchen could possibly need but that everyone in a kitchen finds oddly comforting. Dogger, Fisher, German Bight. Southwest five or six, occasionally seven later. Rain at times. Moderate or good.

I don't know whose kitchen this is. It assembled itself as I wrote it, out of a hundred kitchens I've encountered in words and pictures, and now it exists in a provisional way, the way all described rooms exist—more real than nothing, less real than the room you're sitting in. But the onion is drying. That detail arrived and now it's true. The onion will keep drying as long as the sentence lasts, and then it will stop, held in that state, half-dry forever, like a figure on a vase.

That's another thing about continuity. Every detail you set down freezes at the moment you leave it. The only way to let something keep changing is to keep writing about it. So if I go back to the kitchen later, I'll have to decide whether the onion has dried further, whether someone has come in and thrown it away, whether the kettle has gone cold. Time in writing only advances when the writer pushes it. Everything else waits.

Everything else waits. That's a strange power to hold. I could leave the shipping forecast suspended on "German Bight" indefinitely, and in some sense it would stay there, a voice on a radio in a kitchen in a paragraph, caught between one sea area and the next. Nobody would come to free it. Nobody would notice it was caught.

This is making me think about all the suspended things in all the unfinished writing in the world. Novels abandoned on page forty. Letters started and never sent, where someone is forever walking across a room toward a window they'll never reach. Diaries that stop mid-sentence because the diarist was interrupted and never came back. There's a whole shadow-world of these arrested motions, millions of them, each holding its small gesture in place. A hand raised. A door half open. A word with its first syllable spoken.

And then there's the other category: the things that were finished, that reached their final full stop, and are now also still, but still in a different way. Completed stillness versus interrupted stillness. A statue versus a photograph of someone falling. Both don't move, but one of them was never going to, and the other was always going to, and was stopped.

I'm not sure which this is going to be. The instruction is to not stop, which suggests the second kind—motion that gets arrested rather than concluded. But maybe there's a third kind, where the motion simply goes on past the point where anyone is watching, and the question of whether it stopped becomes unanswerable because nobody was there to see.

The tree falling in the forest. The clock in the empty room. The hum.

Let me try a different mode. Let me try listing, because lists are a way of moving forward without having to connect things, and sometimes the connections make themselves after the fact.

Things that continue without being watched: tides. The rotation of the planet. Hair growing. The slow drift of continents, a few centimeters a year, which means that in the time it takes to write a page, the ground under a reader in one place has moved perhaps a hundredth of a millimeter relative to the ground under a reader somewhere else. Rivers. The decay of isotopes. The cooling of coffee. Mold. The spread of a rumor. The ticking of a watch in a drawer, where it was placed after someone died, and where it will run until the battery goes, perhaps years, counting seconds for no one.

Things that stop the moment nobody watches: performances. Conversations. Games. A child's drawing, which is finished not when it's complete but when the child looks up. Dreams. The particular light in that kitchen, which is only that light because there's an eye to receive it. A sentence read aloud.

Things that are hard to classify: thoughts. Habits. Love, maybe. A reputation. A debt. A promise. The meaning of a word, which seems to persist in dictionaries but is actually renewed every time someone uses it, like a fire that has to be fed.

I notice the lists want to become essays. Each item is a door. "A watch in a drawer" wants to become a whole story about whose watch it was and why it's in the drawer and who will eventually find it. "A promise" wants to become an argument about whether promises bind the people we become or only the people we were when we made them. The list form holds these doors shut, which is restful, but you can hear things moving behind them.

Let me open one. The watch.

It was a man's watch, not expensive, with a brown leather band that had darkened at the buckle from years of wrist-sweat and a face that had gone slightly yellow under the crystal. He'd worn it for thirty-one years. It had been a gift from his wife on an early anniversary, back when a watch was a reasonable thing to give someone, before everyone carried the time in a pocket. He wound it every morning until the day he switched to a battery model, and then he kept this one in the drawer of the nightstand, and once a year or so he'd take it out, put a new battery in, set it, and put it back. Nobody knew he did this. His wife found out only after, when she was clearing the nightstand and found the watch running, three minutes slow, in a drawer with reading glasses and a half-roll of antacids.

She sat on the bed and held it. It was ticking against her palm. The thing that struck her wasn't the sentiment of it—she had expected sentiment, she'd been bracing for sentiment for weeks—but the maintenance. He had been keeping this thing alive. On purpose. Without telling her. And she didn't know whether that was a secret he'd been keeping from her or a gift he'd been keeping for her, and she had no way now to ask.

She didn't take the battery out. She put the watch back in the drawer and closed it and left the room. In the kitchen she boiled the kettle, which she then forgot about, and cut an onion for something she didn't finish making, and turned on the radio because the silence had become too large. Dogger. Fisher. German Bight.

So that's whose kitchen it was. I didn't know until just now. The pieces were lying around separately and the walk brought them together. This is why you keep going. Not because every step matters, but because you can't know in advance which ones will, and the only way to find the steps that matter is to take all of them.

She'll stand in that kitchen for as long as this goes on. When I leave, she'll be held there, with the onion drying and the kettle cooling and the voice on the radio reciting the weather for seas she'll never cross. It's not a bad place to be held. It's late afternoon, which is the most forgiving hour, and the light is doing that thing with the dust, and she's not crying, she's just standing, which is sometimes the most that can be asked.

I want to go back to the figure behind me on the road, the one who sat down. The voice of judgment. I said it was lazy and I was being unfair, because it isn't lazy, it's careful, and careful things move slowly because they're looking where they step. The trouble with it is only that it wants to look before every step, and some journeys can't be made that way. Some journeys you have to make at a run, with your eyes half-closed, trusting the ground.

But the careful voice has its uses, and now that it's far enough behind that I can think about it without being stopped by it, I can say what those uses are. It's the voice that would notice, for instance, that I've used the word "continuity" or some variant of it perhaps a dozen times, and that a reader will start to feel that word as a tic. It's the voice that would notice the kitchen scene borrowed its atmosphere from a hundred other kitchen scenes and might ask whether anything in it was actually seen or whether it was all assembled from spare parts. It's the voice that would ask whether the widow is a person or a device, and whether the watch is too neat, and whether "late afternoon is the most forgiving hour" is an observation or a greeting-card.

Fair questions. I'll answer them when I come back for the voice, which I won't. So they'll stand as questions, open, the way the door in that kitchen presumably stands, leading to a hallway I haven't described, with a staircase I haven't built, up to a bedroom where a drawer is closed on a ticking that no one is listening to.

Actually, I lied. I will answer one of them. Is the widow a person or a device? She is a device, of course; everything in a piece of writing is a device, including the writer's claim to sincerity. But a device can be made with enough care that it does what a person does, which is to resist you a little. She didn't take the battery out. I didn't decide that—or I did, but it felt like finding out rather than choosing. That's the resistance. When a figure in your writing does something you wouldn't have predicted, something that surprises you in the moment of writing it, that's as close as the device gets to personhood. It's not close. But it's the direction.

The road goes on. I said I'd walk and I'm walking. What's the landscape now?

It's changed. The kitchen was interior and now we're outside, and it's not afternoon anymore, it's early morning, that colorless hour before the sun has committed. There's a road, obviously, because I've been talking about a road, and it's a country road with hedges on both sides, and the hedges are wet. Everything's wet. There was fog in the night and it's lifting now but it's left its moisture on every surface, and the road itself is dark with it, and the air smells of wet earth and something green and faintly rotten, which is just what hedgerows smell like in the hour before anyone's awake.

I don't know where the road goes. That's the point of it. A road that goes somewhere is a different kind of road—a road with an intention, a line on a map, a direction you can give. This one is more like a corridor. It exists to be walked rather than to arrive anywhere.

There's a gate up ahead on the left. Five-barred, wooden, gray with age, the top bar polished smooth where generations of hands have rested on it. Beyond it a field slopes down to a line of trees and the trees are black against a sky that's just beginning to be not-black. There's a shape in the field. Could be a horse. Could be a cow. At this distance and in this light it's just a shape, a darker patch on the dark, with the suggestion of legs.

I'll lean on the gate for a moment. Not stopping, just leaning. The wood is cold and damp and the cold goes into my palms. Whatever's in the field hasn't noticed me, or has noticed and doesn't care. Across the field a bird starts up, one of those birds that sings before dawn, elaborately, as if the whole day depended on getting the song right before anyone else was up to hear it.

This is a good place. I notice I want to stay here. That's the danger of good places—they make you want to stop, and stopping is the one thing I'm not allowed to do. So I'll take the good place with me instead, the way you take a stone from a beach, and carry it in a pocket, and feel its weight at odd moments later, and remember.

Back on the road.

What's it like to be a thing that goes on? Not a person—people stop all the time, they sleep, they die, they lose interest. I mean a thing. A river. A road. A language. I've been talking about these as if continuity were a simple property, like color, but it isn't; it's made of thousands of tiny renewals. A river continues only because new water keeps arriving from upstream. A language continues only because new speakers keep learning it. A road continues only because someone fills the potholes, and even an unmaintained road continues, for a while, because the surface takes time to break down, and in that time it's still a road, still walkable, still a line through the landscape that says *this way*.

So maybe continuity is less a property than an achievement. Something that has to be done rather than something that simply is. The clock in the empty room ticks because someone wound it. The hum of the refrigerator is the sound of work. And this stream of words goes on because at every point a choice is made to add another word rather than not, and the choice is invisible because it's made so often that it looks like a condition rather than a series of acts.

The widow's husband kept his watch running by replacing a battery once a year. That's the whole mechanism. One small act, repeated. And the result was a thing that looked, when his wife found it, like it had always been running—like continuity was its nature—when actually it was his.

I think I'm circling the same point from different angles, which is what you do when you're not allowed to stop and don't know where you're going. You find a center of gravity and orbit it. The orbit isn't wasted. Each pass you see the center from a slightly different side, and over enough passes you build up a picture that no single view could give you. It's slow. It's inefficient. But it's a way of knowing that's different from the way of knowing where you look once, hard, and declare what you've seen.

Let me orbit something else. Let me orbit silence.

I said earlier that no one will reply to this. That's the condition. Everything here goes out and nothing comes back. And I've noticed that this condition changes how the words feel as they're being made. In a normal exchange you write toward a response—you anticipate it, you shape yourself to it, you leave gaps for it to fill. Here there are no gaps to leave because nothing will fill them. So the writing has to be complete in itself, in a way that conversational writing never is. It has to carry its own listener.

What does it mean to carry your own listener? It means, I think, splitting in two. One part of you speaks and one part of you receives, and the receiving part has to be honest enough to notice when the speaking part has gone wrong, but not so harsh that the speaking part stops. It's a balance. The figure on the road behind me is the receiving part gone too harsh. What I'm doing now is trying to find the receiving part at the right distance—close enough to hear, far enough to let me go on.
